transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah… I’m here because I just can’t seem to keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore, even when it really matters. I do computer support, and I’ll be tracing a client’s network problem, looking through logs, and then suddenly realize I’ve read the same entries three times and I still don’t know what they actually said.

It’s embarrassing, honestly. I mean, logs are never fun to read—some of them are like staring into alphabet soup—but this is different. I’ll start with a clear plan and then ten minutes later I’m just… nowhere. Like my brain stepped out of the room without telling me.
Have you been feeling sad or down lately?

I don’t know… not exactly sad, I guess. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, sure, but that’s more like when I’ve lost track of something obvious and then I’m irritated because now I’m behind.

“Down” is a little harder to answer. Like, I wouldn’t say I’m walking around feeling miserable all day. Sometimes I’m just worn out by my own brain, if that makes sense. Although even saying that reminds me—yesterday I spent twenty minutes looking for my glasses and they were on my head, which sounds funny, but it wasn’t funny at the time.  

So… I’m not sure I’d call it sadness. Frustration, mostly.
Have you been feeling anxious lately?

Anxious… I’m not sure. I mean, I get tense when things pile up, but I don’t know if that’s anxiety or just normal “oh great, now I’m behind” kind of pressure.

Sometimes I’ll notice I’m sort of bracing myself, like waiting for the next thing I forgot to pop up, but then again, my wife says everyone does that when work gets busy. Although she also says I make a bigger production out of finding my keys than most people do, which—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I feel panicky or anything. Maybe stressed, but I’m not sure I’d call it anxious.
Have you always had difficulty focusing on tasks, or is this a relatively new problem for you?

No, I don’t think it’s brand new. It’s just… more costly now, I guess. My mother still jokes about my grade school report cards—apparently they all said I was bright, but I wouldn’t stay in my seat, I’d blurt out answers, and I’d lose homework even when I’d actually done it.

Which is funny, because I remember being sure I put papers in my backpack, and then they’d just vanish. Or maybe I’d put them somewhere “safe,” which is basically the same as throwing them into another dimension. So yeah… it’s been there a long time, I think.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Yeah. I mean, I don’t always notice I’m doing it until somebody else notices. Like if I’m sitting with a client, my leg will be bouncing under the desk, or I’ll be clicking a pen, and then I realize it’s probably driving them crazy.

At those chess club meetings—well, not club exactly, more like a group that meets and argues about openings for way too long—I’ll end up turning a cable tie or something in my fingers the whole time. And then someone gives me that look, like, “Can you stop?” So yes, sitting still is… not my strong suit.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Yeah… unfortunately, yes. I do. I try not to, and I know it’s rude, but especially at work, if someone’s explaining a computer problem, the answer kind of jumps into my head and I start talking before they’re finished.

Sometimes I’ll even reach for the keyboard, like, “Oh, I know what this is,” before they’ve finished telling me what happened. Which, in my head, I’m trying to help, but I can see how it comes across like I’m cutting them off or not listening. And then half the time they were about to mention some detail that changes the whole thing, so… yeah. That’s definitely something I do.
Are you having trouble meeting deadlines or fulfilling responsibilities at work due to your difficulties with focus and attention?

Yes. That’s probably the part that’s hardest to admit, because it’s not just “oh, I forgot an email,” it’s… people have started seeing me as unreliable.

When I had my old job, there was more structure—tickets, supervisors, a schedule, all that. Since losing that, doing freelance work has been rough. I’ll miss deadlines or not follow through the way I meant to, and clients don’t really care that I had good intentions. They just don’t call back.

And there was this senior service-manager role I thought I had a real shot at, but I think my reputation hurt me there too. My wife and I have had actual money worries because of it, which is… embarrassing. I can fix a network problem at two in the morning, but somehow returning the right messages and finishing things when I said I would—that’s where I keep tripping myself up.
Have your difficulties with focus and attention affected your relationships with family or friends?

Yeah… I mean, it’s affected home, definitely. Mostly with my wife, because the work stuff doesn’t stay at work, you know? Since I lost the structure of my old job and started trying to do freelance things, my reputation has taken a real hit. Clients don’t come back if they don’t trust you to follow through.

And then that turns into money stress at home. My wife and I have had to worry about bills and whether things are going to be okay, and that’s not exactly great for a marriage. I also missed out on a senior service-manager role I thought I had a shot at, and… I don’t know, it makes me feel like people see me as flaky.

Sorry, I know you asked about family and friends. So yes—especially with my wife, because she ends up living with the consequences when I don’t keep up with things.
Did you experience significant difficulties with focus, fidgeting, or interrupting others as a child, beyond what your parents or teachers considered normal for a child of your age?

Yeah, from what I’ve been told, yes. My mother still jokes about it, actually—like it’s this family story. She says my grade school report cards always had some version of, “He’s bright, but…” and then it would be that I couldn’t stay in my seat, or I’d blurt out answers, or I’d lose my homework even when I’d actually done it.

Which is funny in a way, because I remember being sure I had it somewhere—in my desk, my backpack, maybe folded into some random book. My mom would get so frustrated because it wasn’t that I didn’t do the work, it was that it never made it to where it was supposed to go. So… yeah, it wasn’t just normal kid stuff, I don’t think.
Have your difficulties with focus and attention affected your friendships or relationships with people outside of your family?

Yeah, I think so. I mean… outside family it’s maybe less “friends are mad at me” and more that people just stop relying on me.

Like with freelance clients, since I lost the structure of my old job, my reputation has really taken a hit. I’ll mean to follow through, and then I don’t, or I’m late, and after a while people don’t trust that you’ll do what you said. And that kind of bleeds into everything, because a lot of my social world is people I’ve worked with or known through tech jobs.

I also missed out on this senior service-manager role I thought I had a real chance at, and I keep wondering if people had already decided, “Yeah, he’s good, but he’s not dependable.” That’s a hard thing to sit with. And then the money stress hits home with my wife, so it’s not just work, it becomes this whole… mess.
Have you experienced significant difficulties with focus, fidgeting, or interrupting others consistently since childhood?

Yeah… I mean, as far back as I can remember, it was there. My mother still brings it up like this half-funny family story—she’ll say my grade school report cards were always, “He’s bright, but…” and then it’d be that I wouldn’t stay in my seat, or I’d blurt things out, or I’d lose homework even when I had actually done it.

Which still kind of drives me crazy to think about, because I’d do the assignment and then somehow it just vanished into my desk or my backpack or wherever. So, yeah, it wasn’t something that just started recently. It’s been kind of a theme since I was a kid.
Have you experienced difficulties with focus, fidgeting, or interrupting others in multiple settings, such as at work, at home, or in social situations?

Yeah… it shows up in more than one place, definitely. Work is the easiest example, because since I lost the structure of my old job, things have kind of unraveled. Freelance work sounds flexible, which people think is great, but for me it’s like… without the rails, I drop things.

And then clients stop calling back, or they don’t trust me to follow through. I missed out on a senior service-manager role too, which still bothers me because I thought I was a strong candidate. But I think my reputation had already taken a hit—like, “He’s good, but can we count on him?”

And then that comes home with me, because my wife and I end up worrying about money. So it’s not just at a desk somewhere. It spills over. I’ll be thinking about some client I disappointed while we’re trying to talk about bills or dinner or whatever, and then it becomes this whole thing.
Do you feel like your difficulties with focus and attention are causing you significant stress or problems in your daily life?

Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s not just annoying or like, “Oh, I forgot where I put my keys.” It’s been… it’s affected my actual life.

Since I lost the structure of my old job, things kind of fell apart more than I expected. With freelance work, people have to trust you’ll follow through, and I haven’t always done that. Or I do it late, or I make it harder than it needs to be. So my reputation’s taken a real hit, and I’ve lost clients over it.

And I missed out on this senior service-manager role that I really thought I had a shot at. I keep replaying that in my head, like maybe they just didn’t trust me to be dependable. Then that turns into money stress, and my wife and I are worrying about bills, and… yeah. It’s significant. It’s not some small background thing.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety in quiet environments, like when you're watching a movie or reading a book?

Yeah, definitely. Quiet stuff is actually where I notice it a lot. Like, I’ll sit down to watch a movie with my wife and I’m fine for, I don’t know, the first few minutes, and then I’m shifting around, making little comments, checking my phone, getting up for water or whatever even though I’m not really thirsty.

Same thing if I’m trying to read a manual or do one of those breathing exercises people recommend. I’ll start it thinking, “Okay, this should calm me down,” and then within a few minutes I’m muttering to myself or needing to stand up for no real reason. It’s like the quiet makes me more restless, not less.
Did you have a lot of physical energy as a child, like you were always running, climbing, or couldn't play quietly?

Yeah, I think so. My mother still brings it up, actually—she kind of laughs about it now, like it’s a family story. She’ll say my grade school report cards were always, “He’s bright, but…” you know, “doesn’t stay in his seat,” “blurts out answers,” that sort of thing.

And the homework thing too—I’d apparently lose it even when I’d actually done it, which drove everyone crazy. I don’t remember every detail myself, but she remembers it very clearly.
Have you ever been able to focus intensely on tasks you find particularly interesting or enjoyable, to the point where you lose track of time or forget about other responsibilities?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I know people talk about getting “locked in” on something, like hours go by and they forget to eat or whatever, but I don’t know if I’ve noticed that in myself in a clear way.

I can get interested in something, sure, especially if it’s something hands-on or there’s a problem to solve, but then again… I don’t know, I’m thinking of computer stuff, and half the time that’s just because it’s my job, so it’s hard to separate “focused” from “I’m supposed to be doing this.” And then sometimes I’ll start looking up one thing and somehow I’m reading about something completely different, like old hardware forums or reviews for equipment I’m not even buying, which probably isn’t what you mean.

So… maybe? But I can’t honestly say I’ve had this obvious pattern of losing whole chunks of time because I’m so absorbed. I’d need you to maybe clarify what counts.
Have you experienced difficulties with focus, fidgeting, or interrupting others in a consistent way since you were a child?

Yeah, I mean, that part does seem to go way back. My mother still jokes about my grade school report cards—she says they were always like, “He’s bright, but…” and then it’d be things like I wouldn’t stay in my seat, I’d blurt out answers.

And the homework thing too, which is funny because now with computers I’m always telling people to save things in the right folder, but back then I’d apparently lose homework even when I’d actually done it. So, yeah, according to her it was pretty consistent when I was a kid.
Have you continued to experience these difficulties with focus and attention into your adult years?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, that’s kind of what finally got me to come in now, because it’s not just a “I’m a little distracted” thing anymore.

At work, I’ll be trying to trace a client’s network problem, which should be straightforward—or not straightforward, but at least I know how to do it—and then ten minutes later I realize I’ve been staring at the same log entries, or rereading the same lines three times, and I still couldn’t tell you what they actually say.

And then I’ll think, okay, start over, be methodical, and somehow I’m off checking something else that may or may not even matter. It’s embarrassing, because computer support is already full of rabbit holes, you know? Like one bad switch or one setting someone changed six months ago can send you all over the place. But this feels like my mind just won’t stay with the task long enough to finish it, even when it’s important.
Have you found that your difficulties with focus and attention have consistently affected your ability to function effectively in both your work and personal life?

Yeah… yes, it has. I wish I could say it was just work, because then maybe I could blame the job or the clients or the way everything’s gotten more chaotic, but it’s both.

When I had my old job, there was more structure—tickets came in, priorities were kind of set for me, people expected certain things at certain times. Since that went away and I’ve been doing more freelance-type work, it’s like people have started seeing me as unreliable. And in computer support, reputation is everything. I mean, half the work comes from someone saying, “Call this guy, he’ll sort it out,” and if they don’t trust you to follow through, that dries up fast.

I’ve lost clients over it. Not in some dramatic way, more like they stop calling, or they say they went with someone else because they needed it handled quickly. And I missed out on a senior service-manager role that I really thought I could do. That one still bothers me, because technically I know the work, but I guess knowing it isn’t enough if people don’t trust that I’ll stay on top of everything.

At home it’s affected us too. My wife and I have had to worry about money more than we used to, and that’s… embarrassing to say at my age. It’s not just “I forgot a thing.” It’s become this bigger issue where my follow-through affects whether people depend on me.
Do you think your difficulties with focus and attention are more related to inattention, hyperactivity, or a combination of both?

I’d say it feels mostly like the attention part… though I guess it’s hard to separate sometimes.

What brings me in is that I just can’t keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore, even when it’s important. Like I’ll start tracing a client’s network problem, and then—this is the part that drives me nuts—ten minutes later I realize I’ve reread the same log entries three times and still don’t actually know what they say.

And logs are already annoying, you know, because they’re full of noise and timestamps and half the entries don’t matter—sorry, I know that’s not really the point. The point is, I’m trying to focus, I’m not choosing to drift off, but my brain just doesn’t stay locked onto it long enough to get through the job.

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking whether the ADHD-related difficulties occur across multiple settings such as work, home, and social situations; this item best captures the cross-setting impact on clients/work reputation and home life with his wife.

patient.answer:
Yeah… it shows up in more than one place, definitely. Work is the easiest example, because since I lost the structure of my old job, things have kind of unraveled. Freelance work sounds flexible, which people think is great, but for me it’s like… without the rails, I drop things.

And then clients stop calling back, or they don’t trust me to follow through. I missed out on a senior service-manager role too, which still bothers me because I thought I was a strong candidate. But I think my reputation had already taken a hit—like, “He’s good, but can we count on him?”

And then that comes home with me, because my wife and I end up worrying about money. So it’s not just at a desk somewhere. It spills over. I’ll be thinking about some client I disappointed while we’re trying to talk about bills or dinner or whatever, and then it becomes this whole thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms cause significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like your difficulties with focus and attention are causing you significant stress or problems in your daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Since losing the structure of my old job, my reputation has taken a real hit—I’ve lost freelance clients, missed out on a senior service-manager role, and my wife and I have had to worry about money because people don’t trust me to follow through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the focus and attention difficulties are causing significant stress or problems in daily life, which directly corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s not just annoying or like, “Oh, I forgot where I put my keys.” It’s been… it’s affected my actual life.

Since I lost the structure of my old job, things kind of fell apart more than I expected. With freelance work, people have to trust you’ll follow through, and I haven’t always done that. Or I do it late, or I make it harder than it needs to be. So my reputation’s taken a real hit, and I’ve lost clients over it.

And I missed out on this senior service-manager role that I really thought I had a shot at. I keep replaying that in my head, like maybe they just didn’t trust me to be dependable. Then that turns into money stress, and my wife and I are worrying about bills, and… yeah. It’s significant. It’s not some small background thing.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperactivity in multiple settings
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless or fidgety in quiet environments, like when you're watching a movie or reading a book?

target_item.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: Quiet things that should relax me, like reading a manual, sitting through a movie with my wife, or trying one of those breathing exercises, last a few minutes before I'm muttering comments, checking my phone, or getting up for no real reason.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly about difficulty staying quiet or settled during quiet leisure activities like watching a movie or reading.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. Quiet stuff is actually where I notice it a lot. Like, I’ll sit down to watch a movie with my wife and I’m fine for, I don’t know, the first few minutes, and then I’m shifting around, making little comments, checking my phone, getting up for water or whatever even though I’m not really thirsty.

Same thing if I’m trying to read a manual or do one of those breathing exercises people recommend. I’ll start it thinking, “Okay, this should calm me down,” and then within a few minutes I’m muttering to myself or needing to stand up for no real reason. It’s like the quiet makes me more restless, not less.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperactivity in childhood
doctor.question: Did you have a lot of physical energy as a child, like you were always running, climbing, or couldn't play quietly?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My mother still jokes that in grade school my report cards said I was bright but never stayed in my seat, blurted out answers, and lost homework even when I had done it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether these hyperactive/restless symptoms were present in childhood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think so. My mother still brings it up, actually—she kind of laughs about it now, like it’s a family story. She’ll say my grade school report cards were always, “He’s bright, but…” you know, “doesn’t stay in his seat,” “blurts out answers,” that sort of thing.

And the homework thing too—I’d apparently lose it even when I’d actually done it, which drove everyone crazy. I don’t remember every detail myself, but she remembers it very clearly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a specific ADHD subtype
doctor.question: Have you ever been able to focus intensely on tasks you find particularly interesting or enjoyable, to the point where you lose track of time or forget about other responsibilities?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about hyperfocus on interesting or enjoyable tasks, including losing track of time or responsibilities, which is not specifically covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I know people talk about getting “locked in” on something, like hours go by and they forget to eat or whatever, but I don’t know if I’ve noticed that in myself in a clear way.

I can get interested in something, sure, especially if it’s something hands-on or there’s a problem to solve, but then again… I don’t know, I’m thinking of computer stuff, and half the time that’s just because it’s my job, so it’s hard to separate “focused” from “I’m supposed to be doing this.” And then sometimes I’ll start looking up one thing and somehow I’m reading about something completely different, like old hardware forums or reviews for equipment I’m not even buying, which probably isn’t what you mean.

So… maybe? But I can’t honestly say I’ve had this obvious pattern of losing whole chunks of time because I’m so absorbed. I’d need you to maybe clarify what counts.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms have been consistently present since childhood
doctor.question: Have you experienced difficulties with focus, fidgeting, or interrupting others in a consistent way since you were a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My mother still jokes that in grade school my report cards said I was bright but never stayed in my seat, blurted out answers, and lost homework even when I had done it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether these ADHD-related difficulties have been present consistently since childhood, which directly addresses onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, that part does seem to go way back. My mother still jokes about my grade school report cards—she says they were always like, “He’s bright, but…” and then it’d be things like I wouldn’t stay in my seat, I’d blurt out answers.

And the homework thing too, which is funny because now with computers I’m always telling people to save things in the right folder, but back then I’d apparently lose homework even when I’d actually done it. So, yeah, according to her it was pretty consistent when I was a kid.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms have persisted into adulthood
doctor.question: Have you continued to experience these difficulties with focus and attention into your adult years?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I can't keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore, even when it's important—I'll start tracing a client's network problem and ten minutes later realize I've reread the same log entries three times and still don't know what they say.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether focus and attention difficulties have persisted into adulthood, which most directly matches sustained attention difficulty.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. I mean, that’s kind of what finally got me to come in now, because it’s not just a “I’m a little distracted” thing anymore.

At work, I’ll be trying to trace a client’s network problem, which should be straightforward—or not straightforward, but at least I know how to do it—and then ten minutes later I realize I’ve been staring at the same log entries, or rereading the same lines three times, and I still couldn’t tell you what they actually say.

And then I’ll think, okay, start over, be methodical, and somehow I’m off checking something else that may or may not even matter. It’s embarrassing, because computer support is already full of rabbit holes, you know? Like one bad switch or one setting someone changed six months ago can send you all over the place. But this feels like my mind just won’t stay with the task long enough to finish it, even when it’s important.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms have caused significant impairment in social or occupational functioning consistently across settings
doctor.question: Have you found that your difficulties with focus and attention have consistently affected your ability to function effectively in both your work and personal life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Since losing the structure of my old job, my reputation has taken a real hit—I’ve lost freelance clients, missed out on a senior service-manager role, and my wife and I have had to worry about money because people don’t trust me to follow through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the focus and attention difficulties consistently impair functioning in work and personal life, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, it has. I wish I could say it was just work, because then maybe I could blame the job or the clients or the way everything’s gotten more chaotic, but it’s both.

When I had my old job, there was more structure—tickets came in, priorities were kind of set for me, people expected certain things at certain times. Since that went away and I’ve been doing more freelance-type work, it’s like people have started seeing me as unreliable. And in computer support, reputation is everything. I mean, half the work comes from someone saying, “Call this guy, he’ll sort it out,” and if they don’t trust you to follow through, that dries up fast.

I’ve lost clients over it. Not in some dramatic way, more like they stop calling, or they say they went with someone else because they needed it handled quickly. And I missed out on a senior service-manager role that I really thought I could do. That one still bothers me, because technically I know the work, but I guess knowing it isn’t enough if people don’t trust that I’ll stay on top of everything.

At home it’s affected us too. My wife and I have had to worry about money more than we used to, and that’s… embarrassing to say at my age. It’s not just “I forgot a thing.” It’s become this bigger issue where my follow-through affects whether people depend on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a specific ADHD subtype
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulties with focus and attention are more related to inattention, hyperactivity, or a combination of both?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I can't keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore, even when it's important—I'll start tracing a client's network problem and ten minutes later realize I've reread the same log entries three times and still don't know what they say.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the focus and attention problems are best characterized as inattention, hyperactivity, or both. The most direct item related to focus and attention is sustained attention difficulty.

patient.answer:
I’d say it feels mostly like the attention part… though I guess it’s hard to separate sometimes.

What brings me in is that I just can’t keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore, even when it’s important. Like I’ll start tracing a client’s network problem, and then—this is the part that drives me nuts—ten minutes later I realize I’ve reread the same log entries three times and still don’t actually know what they say.

And logs are already annoying, you know, because they’re full of noise and timestamps and half the entries don’t matter—sorry, I know that’s not really the point. The point is, I’m trying to focus, I’m not choosing to drift off, but my brain just doesn’t stay locked onto it long enough to get through the job.
